title: Kamala
focus: entering the city and learning love

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha dreams of Govinda becoming a woman, crosses a river with a kind ferryman (Vasudeva) who predicts his return, and reaches a city where he sees the beautiful courtesan Kamala. She tells him he needs fine clothes, shoes and money; he learns quickly and, through her, gains a position with the merchant Kamaswami. Kamala becomes his teacher in love.

vocabulary.definition: To remove from on board a vessel
vocabulary.context: “I thank you, my benefactor,” spoke Siddhartha, disembarking on the other side of the river.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disembark”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + bark (Late Latin barca, "small boat"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The shell of any marine mollusk
vocabulary.context: In front of the mud cottages, children were rolling about in the street, were playing with pumpkinseeds and seashells, screamed and wrestled, but they all timidly fled from the unknown Samana.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “seashell”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being distinguished by sex
vocabulary.context: Siddhartha also felt desire and felt the source of his sexuality moving; but since he had never touched a woman before, he hesitated for a moment, while his hands were already prepared to reach out for her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sexuality”: se- (Latin se-, "apart") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To shine with a tremulous or intermittent light
vocabulary.context: It intoxicated him and rendered him unconscious.—When Siddhartha woke up, the pale river shimmered through the door of the hut, and in the forest, a dark call of an owl resounded deeply and pleasantly.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “shimmer”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Many young men come to me, and there are also sons of Brahmins among them, but they come in beautiful clothes, they come in fine shoes, they have perfume in their hair and money in their pouches.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pouch”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: An artificial reservoir or tank for holding water, beer, or other liquids
vocabulary.context: Differently the sun burnt the head, differently the shade of the forest cooled him down, differently the stream and the cistern, the pumpkin and the banana tasted.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cistern”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A bow or arch exhibiting, in concentric bands, the several colors of the spectrum, and formed in the part of the…
vocabulary.context: He saw trees, stars, animals, clouds, rainbows, rocks, herbs, flowers, stream and river, the glistening dew in the bushes in the morning, distant high mountains which were blue and pale, birds sang and bees, wind silverishly blew through the rice field.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rainbow”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To introduce by a first act
vocabulary.context: While talking, she put her left foot on his right one and made a movement as a woman does who would want to initiate that kind of sexual pleasure with a man, which the textbooks call “climbing a tree.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “initiate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To strike together so as to produce a ringing metallic sound
vocabulary.context: Kamala loudly clapped her hands, so that the golden bracelets clanged.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “clang”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: (Zoöl.) Any one of several species of carnivorous animals inhabiting Africa and Asia, related to the dog and wolf
vocabulary.context: “Why should I be afraid of a Samana, a stupid Samana from the forest, who is coming from the jackals and doesn’t even know yet what women are?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “jackal”: -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Courtesans in ancient India could be educated, wealthy and respected.

significance: The ferryman's prophecy and the river crossing foreshadow the novel's final setting.
discussionQuestions: Siddhartha says he can 'think, wait and fast.' Why are these powerful skills?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with love and attachment?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Kamala,” how does Hesse show entering the city and learning love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Kamala develops the idea of entering the city and learning love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses characterization in Kamala to complicate the reader's understanding of entering the city and learning love. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Kamala within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of entering the city and learning love responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Kamala as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of entering the city and learning love. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “I thank you, my benefactor,” spoke Siddhartha, disembarking on the other side of the river. “I have no gift I could give you for your hospitality, my dear, and also no payment for your work. I am a man without a home, a son of a Brahmin and a Samana.”

annotationFocus.label: Symbolism

annotationFocus.label: Setting

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Siddhartha says he can 'think, wait and fast.' Why are these powerful skills? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are disembarking, seashells, sexuality, shimmered, pouches. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““I thank you, my benefactor,” spoke Siddhartha, disembarking on the other side of the river.” Webster's says: To remove from on board a vessel. Now the word history: “disembark”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + bark (Late Latin barca, "small boat"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “seashell”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “sexuality”: se- (Latin se-, "apart") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Courtesans in ancient India could be educated, wealthy and respected. Why does this chapter matter? The ferryman's prophecy and the river crossing foreshadow the novel's final setting. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to entering the city and learning love.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Symbolism, Setting.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “I thank you, my benefactor,” spoke Siddhartha, disembarking on the other side of the river. “I have no gift I could give you for your hospitality, my dear, and also no payment for your work. I am a man without a home, a son of a Brahmin and a Samana.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Symbolism, Setting: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Kamala,” how does Hesse show entering the city and learning love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about entering the city and learning love, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes entering the city and learning love. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
